newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Ross urges Israel, PLO unite against common threat.
newsitem.headline: Ross urges Israel, PLO unite against common threat.

text.p: U.S. envoy Dennis Ross urged Israelis and Palestinians on Monday to work as partners against a "common threat" from militants following a suicide attack in Jerusalem that has plunged peacemaking deep into crisis.
Ross, on the second day of his mission, said the two sides had come a step closer to reviving security ties but cautioned that success would be measured by results.
U.S., Palestinian and Israeli security officials met in the West Bank Ramallah self-rule enclave on Monday night, PLO officials said. No details were available from that meeting.
Ross and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat also met in Ramallah. Arafat adviser Nabil Abu Rdainah told Reuters after the meeting:

"We demand linking the security efforts to progress on the political issues so that we can resolve the crisis. Any progress on the security level without equal progress on the political track will be insufficient."
That linkage would not please Israel.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has accused Arafat of having a "revolving door" for militants in his prisons.
He has conditioned resuming peace talks and easing economic and security sanctions imposed on the West Bank and Gaza Strip after the bombings on a crackdown by the Palestinian Authority.
Arafat says he has met his responsibilities on security and accuses Netanyahu of using the Jerusalem bombings as an excuse to inflict "collective punishment" on Palestinians.
"We are looking for results. They have to fight terrorism. Period," Netanyahu said in an interview with the MSNBC television.
Ross earlier in the day said: "We're not looking for meetings as an end in themselves. We're looking for results."
"Security is something that serves Israeli interests and Palestinian interests. You have a common threat and you have a common enemy and it's important to deal with that as partners."
Within hours of his arrival on Sunday, Ross brought together Arafat and Israeli officials for the first time since two Arab suicide bombers attacked an Israeli market on July 30.
The death toll from the attack rose to 16, including the two Moslem militants, with the death in hospital on Monday of a 49-year-old Israeli man who was gravely injured in the blast.
PLO officials said the U.S.-Israeli-PLO meeting late on Sunday had enabled the sides to exchange information on the attack and to coordinate security.
But neither Israel nor the Palestinians sounded confident progress towards salvaging peace efforts would come swiftly.
Netanyahu's cabinet secretary Danny Naveh told Israel Radio:

"We very much hope the American envoy Ross's efforts will yield results but until now we've seen no real change on the part of the Palestinian Authority in everything that has to do with its war on terrorism."
"We are insisting that the main issue is the political issue," Abu Rdainah told Israel Radio.
"Unless they understand there is a peace agreement signed by the Palestinian Authority and the Israeli authorities, unless it's implemented fully and accurately, the crisis will carry on," he said.

In Amman, the Islamic militant group Hamas warned Arafat against heeding Israel's demands. "It would be dangerous, not just for him...It would lead to Palestinians fighting Palestinians," Hamas spokesman Ibrahim Ghoshe said.

Tayeb Abdel-Rahim, an Arafat aide, said in a statement the Palestinian Authority "will not allow Ghoshe or the likes of him to play with the fate of our people or harm the Authority or threaten it with terrorism or civil war".
Netanyahu has said Israel has indications Hamas carried out the attack even though Israeli and Palestinian officials question the authenticity of a Hamas claim of responsibility.
In Gaza City, thousands of Palestinian protesters marched down the main street demanding Israel free their imprisoned sons and end the closure imposed on Palestinians after the attack.

Trouble also flared briefly just outside the Palestinian-ruled West Bank town of Ramallah when about 50 youths burned tyres and tried to throw stones at Israeli soldiers. Palestinian police entered Israeli-controlled territory to disperse the protesters.
Ross has been preparing for U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright's first trip to the region, expected at the end of the month provided progress is made on security. He said:
"There has to be a basis of security to be able to underpin and move the peace process and there has to be a political dimension ultimately for the peace process to succeed."
Peace talks had already been in crisis over a Jewish settlement Israel began building in Arab East Jerusalem in March. Palestinians want construction halted.
